title: Death for Manstealing
kjv_text: And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
summary: Kidnapping a person for sale — or being caught holding the victim — is a capital offense.
original_audience: Israelites; the target is slave-raiding and trafficking of community members.
immediate_context: In the capital list; the one property crime the code treats as capital, because the 'property' is a person.
historical_context: Hammurabi 14 also makes kidnapping capital. Deut 24:7 restricts the biblical rule to stealing 'of his brethren' — Israelites — leaving foreign slave-trading in the Lev 25:44 lane. The Joseph narrative (Gen 37) is the canon's own manstealing case study, unprosecuted.
exceptions: By Deut 24:7's wording, victims outside the covenant community fall outside the statute — the loophole on which transatlantic slavery's apologists later built.
nt_passages: 1 Timothy 1:10 — 'menstealers' listed among the lawless; the verse abolitionists preached
Revelation 18:13 — Babylon's cargo includes 'slaves, and souls of men'

internal_contradictions.issue: Does God approve of slavery? Manstealing is death, yet buying the stolen (if foreign-sourced) is lawful commerce under Lev 25:44 — the code executes the thief and licenses the fence.

usofc_implementation: Enforced vigorously and advertised as the regime's anti-trafficking crown jewel — with Deut 24:7's 'brethren' limit quietly imported: full capital protection for communicant citizens, a lesser 'unlawful conveyance' offense when victims are non-covenant aliens. The OSO's guest-labor pipeline is never, officially, in scope.
constitutional_analogue: Federal kidnapping statute plus the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, tiered by religious citizenship — an equal-protection abyss.
scene_ideas: A trafficking prosecutor discovering her airtight capital case downgrades the moment the victim's baptism record can't be produced.
A 1 Timothy 1:10 abolitionist cell that hunts OSO labor recruiters with subpoenas.
satirical_uses: The anti-trafficking billboard and the guest-worker terminal share a highway exit.
